softwareProject.settings module

Django settings for softwareProject project.

This module contains all configuration settings for the expense tracking application, including database configuration, installed apps, middleware, templates, static files, and security settings.

Generated by ‘django-admin startproject’ using Django 6.0.4.

For more information on this file, see:

https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.0/topics/settings/

For the full list of settings and their values, see:

https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.0/ref/settings/

Environment:

Development configuration - NOT suitable for production DEBUG=True - Do not use in production environment

Security Warning:

This settings file contains sensitive information (SECRET_KEY). Never commit this file to public repositories in production. Use environment variables for production deployments.

softwareProject.settings.BASE_DIR = WindowsPath('D:/django project documentation')

Base directory of the Django project.

Calculated as the parent directory of the directory containing this file. Used as reference point for constructing absolute paths throughout settings.

Example

BASE_DIR / ‘db.sqlite3’ → /path/to/project/db.sqlite3 BASE_DIR / ‘static’ → /path/to/project/static

Type: pathlib.Path object (cross-platform path handling)

softwareProject.settings.SECRET_KEY = 'django-insecure-v1k8^#l$kaweg)2_ril^tdm%10u5)roj6-s$r1ay^v%ctao#xr'

Secret key for cryptographic signing.

Purpose:

  • Session signing

  • CSRF protection

  • Password reset tokens

  • Message signing

  • Cryptographic hashing

Security Warning:

This is a development key (starts with ‘django-insecure’).

Production Requirements:

Never commit production secret keys to version control.

softwareProject.settings.DEBUG = True

Debug mode setting.

When True (Development):

  • Shows detailed error pages with tracebacks

  • Enables automatic template reloading

  • Static files served by Django

  • SQL queries logged

  • Displays Python variables in error pages

When False (Production):

  • Shows generic error pages (404, 500)

  • Disables detailed error reporting

  • Requires proper static file serving (nginx/CDN)

  • Should implement ALLOWED_HOSTS

Security Warning:

MUST be set to False in production to prevent: - Code execution disclosure - Sensitive data leaks - Cross-site scripting vulnerabilities - Database query exposure

softwareProject.settings.ALLOWED_HOSTS = []

List of host/domain names that Django can serve.

Development:

Empty list means localhost/127.0.0.1 and ‘localhost’ only (Not allowed when DEBUG=False)

Production Requirements:

Must list all domains serving the application: Example: ALLOWED_HOSTS = [‘example.com’, ‘www.example.com’, ‘your-domain.com’]

Security:

Prevents HTTP Host header attacks Django will reject requests with invalid Host headers

To allow all hosts (not recommended):

ALLOWED_HOSTS = [‘*’]

softwareProject.settings.INSTALLED_APPS = ['django.contrib.admin', 'django.contrib.auth', 'django.contrib.contenttypes', 'django.contrib.sessions', 'django.contrib.messages', 'django.contrib.staticfiles', 'register_login', 'expensesApp']

List of installed Django applications.

Application categories:

  1. Django Built-in: Core framework functionality

  2. Custom Apps: Project-specific functionality

Order Notes:

  • Apps are loaded in the order listed

  • Custom apps should come after Django core apps

  • App names must match directory names in project

Each app provides:

  • Models (database tables)

  • Views (business logic)

  • Templates (HTML rendering)

  • Static files (CSS/JS)

  • URL configurations

  • Management commands (optional)

softwareProject.settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL = 'register_login.userRegistration'

Custom user model for authentication.

Replaces Django’s default User model with custom userRegistration model.

Why Custom User Model:

  • Added is_first_login field for onboarding workflow

  • Custom username field with length constraints

  • Future expansion capabilities (can add more fields later)

  • Best practice: Always use custom user model in new projects

Important

Must be set before creating any migrations Changing this after migrations requires database modifications

Usage:

from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model User = get_user_model() # Returns userRegistration class

Example in views:

user = get_user_model().objects.get(id=1)

softwareProject.settings.MIDDLEWARE = ['django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware', 'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware', 'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware', 'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware', 'django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware', 'django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware', 'django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware']

Request/response middleware pipeline.

Middleware execution order:

Request → Each middleware processes request (top to bottom) Response ← Each middleware processes response (bottom to top)

Middleware Purposes:

  1. Security: Adds security headers, HSTS, XSS protection

  2. Sessions: Manages user session data and cookies

  3. Common: Handles URL rewriting, ETags, content negotiation

  4. CSRF: Protects against cross-site request forgery attacks

  5. Authentication: Associates logged-in users with requests

  6. Messages: Handles one-time flash messages for user feedback

  7. XFrame: Prevents clickjacking attacks (page embedding)

Notes

Order is extremely important - do not change unless you understand dependencies CSRF middleware must come after SessionMiddleware Authentication middleware must come after SessionMiddleware

Custom template directory path.

Points to project-level templates directory for shared templates.

Calculated as: softwareProject/templates/ Type: String (absolute path)

Purpose:

  • Store base templates used across multiple apps

  • Override app templates when needed

  • Keep organization-wide templates in one location

Example Structure:

softwareProject/templates/ ├── base.html # Base template for all pages ├── main.html # Home page template └── includes/ # Reusable template components

softwareProject.settings.TEMPLATES = [{'APP_DIRS': True, 'BACKEND': 'django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates', 'DIRS': ['D:\\django project documentation\\softwareProject/templates'], 'OPTIONS': {'context_processors': ['django.template.context_processors.request', 'django.contrib.auth.context_processors.auth', 'django.contrib.messages.context_processors.messages']}}]

Template engine configuration.

Settings for Django’s template system:

BACKEND:

DjangoTemplates - Default template engine (other options: Jinja2)

DIRS:

List of directories to search for templates Includes project-level TEMP_DIR for shared templates

APP_DIRS:

True - Searches for templates in ‘templates’ subdirectory of each app

Context Processors:

  • request: Makes request object available as {{ request }}

  • auth: Makes user object available as {{ user }}

  • messages: Makes flash messages available as {% messages %}

Template search order:

  1. DIRS directories (project-level templates) - highest priority

  2. App directories (each app’s templates folder) - lower priority

softwareProject.settings.DATABASES = {'default': {'ATOMIC_REQUESTS': False, 'AUTOCOMMIT': True, 'CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS': False, 'CONN_MAX_AGE': 0, 'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3', 'HOST': '', 'NAME': WindowsPath('D:/django project documentation/db.sqlite3'), 'OPTIONS': {}, 'PASSWORD': '', 'PORT': '', 'TEST': {'CHARSET': None, 'COLLATION': None, 'MIGRATE': True, 'MIRROR': None, 'NAME': None}, 'TIME_ZONE': None, 'USER': ''}}

Database configuration.

Current Configuration (Development):

ENGINE: SQLite3 (file-based database, no separate server) NAME: db.sqlite3 in project root

Advantages of SQLite:

  • Zero configuration (no database server to install)

  • File-based, easy to backup (just copy the file)

  • Great for development and testing

  • No network latency

  • Works on any platform

Disadvantages:

  • Not suitable for high concurrency

  • Limited features compared to PostgreSQL/MySQL

  • Not recommended for production

Production Recommendation:

Use PostgreSQL for production:

DATABASES = {
‘default’: {

‘ENGINE’: ‘django.db.backends.postgresql’, ‘NAME’: ‘expenses_db’, ‘USER’: ‘db_user’, ‘PASSWORD’: ‘secure_password’, ‘HOST’: ‘localhost’, ‘PORT’: ‘5432’,

}

}

Using Environment Variables (recommended for production):

import os DATABASES = {

‘default’: {

‘ENGINE’: ‘django.db.backends.postgresql’, ‘NAME’: os.environ.get(‘DB_NAME’, ‘expenses_db’), ‘USER’: os.environ.get(‘DB_USER’, ‘postgres’), ‘PASSWORD’: os.environ.get(‘DB_PASSWORD’, ‘’), ‘HOST’: os.environ.get(‘DB_HOST’, ‘localhost’), ‘PORT’: os.environ.get(‘DB_PORT’, ‘5432’),

}

}

softwareProject.settings.AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS = [{'NAME': 'django.contrib.auth.password_validation.UserAttributeSimilarityValidator'}, {'NAME': 'django.contrib.auth.password_validation.MinimumLengthValidator'}, {'NAME': 'django.contrib.auth.password_validation.CommonPasswordValidator'}, {'NAME': 'django.contrib.auth.password_validation.NumericPasswordValidator'}]

Password validation rules.

These validators work alongside custom form validators (like the 8-20 character validation in registration form).

Validators enforce password strength requirements:

  1. UserAttributeSimilarityValidator: - Prevents passwords similar to username, email, etc. - Checks for common patterns and similarities - Example: Password ‘john123’ for username ‘john’ would be rejected

  2. MinimumLengthValidator: - Enforces minimum password length (default: 8 characters) - Can be customized with OPTIONS:

    {‘OPTIONS’: {‘min_length’: 12}}

  3. CommonPasswordValidator: - Blocks commonly used passwords - Uses list of 20,000 common passwords - Examples: ‘password123’, ‘qwerty’, ‘admin’, ‘12345678’

  4. NumericPasswordValidator: - Prevents entirely numeric passwords - Blocks passwords like ‘12345678’ or ‘11111111’

Custom Validator Example:

Add custom options to MinimumLengthValidator: {

‘NAME’: ‘django.contrib.auth.password_validation.MinimumLengthValidator’, ‘OPTIONS’: {‘min_length’: 12}

}

Note

These validators apply to all password changes (admin, user forms). Custom form validators (8-20 chars) are additional restrictions.

softwareProject.settings.TIME_ZONE = 'UTC'

Time zone for date/time storage and display.

Default: ‘UTC’ (Coordinated Universal Time) - recommended for consistency

Other common options:

  • ‘America/New_York’ (Eastern Time)

  • ‘America/Chicago’ (Central Time)

  • ‘America/Los_Angeles’ (Pacific Time)

  • ‘Europe/London’ (UK Time)

  • ‘Asia/Dubai’ (GST)

  • ‘Asia/Tokyo’ (Japan Time)

Warning

Changing after database creation requires data migration. All dates/times are stored in UTC in database regardless of this setting. This setting only affects display conversion.

softwareProject.settings.USE_I18N = True

Enable internationalization (i18n) support.

When True:

  • Django’s translation system is active

  • {% trans %} template tags work

  • Language detection middleware can be used

  • Translation files (.po, .mo) are loaded

Set to False if application will only use one language (improves performance).

softwareProject.settings.USE_TZ = True

Enable timezone-aware datetime handling.

When True (RECOMMENDED):

  • datetime objects are timezone-aware

  • Django uses TIME_ZONE for conversion

  • Times are stored in UTC in database

  • Best for user-facing applications

When False (Legacy):

  • datetime objects are naive (no timezone)

  • All times are stored in TIME_ZONE setting

  • Can cause issues with daylight saving time

Best Practice:

Keep as True for proper datetime handling across timezones. Users in different time zones will see corrected times.

softwareProject.settings.STATICFILES_DIRS = [WindowsPath('D:/django project documentation/static')]

Additional directories where Django looks for static files.

Beyond the ‘static’ directory in each app, these directories are also searched.

Purpose:

  • Project-wide static files (shared across apps)

  • Files that don’t belong to a specific app

  • Third-party static files (outside of installed apps)

Examples

BASE_DIR / ‘static’ contains:

  • css/main.css (project-wide CSS)

  • js/global.js (global JavaScript)

  • images/logo.png (site logo)

  • favicon.ico (browser icon)

Search Order (collectstatic command):

  1. STATICFILES_DIRS directories

  2. Static directories in each INSTALLED_APPS

Note

The collectstatic command will copy all static files found in these directories to STATIC_ROOT for production.

softwareProject.settings.STATIC_ROOT = WindowsPath('D:/django project documentation/staticfiles')

Directory where static files are collected for production.

This is the destination directory for the ‘collectstatic’ management command.

Purpose:

  1. Collect all static files from all apps and directories

  2. Create a single directory for production serving

  3. Organize static files for web server configuration

Management Command:

python manage.py collectstatic - Copies all static files to STATIC_ROOT directory - Must be run before every production deployment

Important

  • Should be an empty directory before collectstatic

  • Do NOT commit this directory to version control

  • Web server should point to this directory for static files

  • Should be excluded in .gitignore: ‘staticfiles/’

Example Nginx Configuration:
location /static/ {

alias /path/to/project/staticfiles/; expires 30d; # Cache static files for 30 days

}

softwareProject.settings.MEDIA_ROOT = WindowsPath('D:/django project documentation/static/images')

Absolute path to directory where user-uploaded media files are stored.

Purpose:

  • Store uploaded files (category icons, user avatars, etc.)

  • Separate location from static files

  • Django writes files here when users upload

Directory Structure:

  • Category icons: MEDIA_ROOT/category_name/icon.png

  • User uploads organized by app

Example

Category icon upload → MEDIA_ROOT/icons/food.png Full path: /project/static/images/icons/food.png

Production Considerations:

  • DO NOT serve with Django in production (inefficient)

  • Configure web server (nginx) to serve from this directory

  • Consider cloud storage (AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage) for scaling

Example nginx configuration: location /images/ {

alias /path/to/project/static/images/; expires 30d;

}

Security:

  • Implement file validation (type, size, content) in forms

  • Scan uploads for malware in production

  • Consider using django-storages for cloud storage

Warning

  • User uploads can consume significant disk space

  • Implement cleanup for old/unused files

  • Consider rate limiting for uploads

softwareProject.urls module

Main Project URL Configuration for softwareProject.

This module defines the top-level URL patterns for the entire expense tracking application. It routes incoming requests to appropriate app-level URL configurations and serves static/media files during development.

The urlpatterns list routes URLs to views. For more information please see:

https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.0/topics/http/urls/

URL Structure:

/admin/ - Django admin interface /register/ - User registration (from register_login) /login/ - User login (from register_login) /logout/ - User logout (from register_login) /addExpense/ - Add new expense (from expensesApp) /categories/ - Manage categories (from expensesApp) /setCycle/ - Budget cycle setup (from expensesApp) /insights/ - Spending insights (from expensesApp) /home/ - Main dashboard

Examples

Function views:

  1. Add import: from my_app import views

  2. Add URL: path(‘’, views.home, name=’home’)

Class-based views:

  1. Add import: from other_app.views import Home

  2. Add URL: path(‘’, Home.as_view(), name=’home’)

Including another URLconf:

  1. Import include(): from django.urls import include, path

  2. Add URL: path(‘blog/’, include(‘blog.urls’))

softwareProject.views module

Main Application Views Module.

This module contains the core views for the root application, including the main dashboard/home page that displays budget overview, spending metrics, and daily spending limits for authenticated users.

Key Features:

  • Budget cycle overview and status

  • Safe daily limit calculation (server-side)

  • Spending progress tracking with percentage

  • Daily spending alerts

  • Cycle status monitoring (active, ended, overspent)

All views are protected by @login_required decorator to ensure only authenticated users can access the dashboard.

softwareProject.views.home(request)[source]

Main dashboard view displaying user’s budget cycle status and spending metrics.

This view serves as the primary dashboard for authenticated users, showing real-time budget information including total spent, remaining budget, safe daily limit, and spending progress. All calculations are performed server-side with no JavaScript required for maximum compatibility and security.

Parameters:

request – HTTP request object from authenticated user

Returns:

Rendered main.html template with comprehensive budget context data

Formula Calculations:

total_spent = SUM(expense.amount) for current cycle remaining_budget = total_allowance - total_spent days_remaining = MAX((end_date - today).days + 1, 1) safe_daily_limit = remaining_budget / days_remaining progress_percent = MIN((total_spent / total_allowance) * 100, 100)

Status Definitions:

  • ‘no_cycle’: User has no active budget cycle configured

  • ‘active’: Cycle is within date range and budget not exceeded

  • ‘ended’: Current date is past cycle end date

  • ‘overspent’: Total spending has exceeded total allowance

Alert Conditions:

  • Shows warning when today_spent > safe_daily_limit (exceeds daily limit)

  • Shows “Cycle Ended” message when today > end_date

  • Shows “Budget Exceeded” message when remaining_budget < 0

  • Shows setup prompt when no cycle exists

Context Variables:

cycle (Cycle/None): Current active budget cycle object safe_daily_limit (Decimal/None): Recommended daily spending limit total_spent (Decimal): Total amount spent in current cycle remaining_budget (Decimal/None): Budget remaining after expenses days_remaining (int/None): Number of days left in cycle (minimum 1) progress_percent (int): Percentage of budget used (0-100) status (str): Cycle status - ‘active’, ‘ended’, ‘overspent’, ‘no_cycle’ today_spent (Decimal): Total amount spent today over_daily_limit (bool): Whether today’s spending exceeds safe limit

Example Output:
If user has a $1000 budget for 30 days and spent $200:

total_spent = 200.00 remaining_budget = 800.00 days_remaining = 25 (assuming 5 days passed) safe_daily_limit = 32.00 (800 / 25) progress_percent = 20% status = ‘active’

Security:

  • @login_required ensures only authenticated users can access

  • Each user only sees their own data via request.user filtering

  • No sensitive data exposed to unauthenticated users

Performance Notes:
  • Two database queries maximum:

    1. Get active cycle

    2. Sum of expenses for cycle

    3. Sum of today’s expenses (included in same query pattern)

  • Uses aggregation for efficient database operations

  • Decimal operations for precise monetary calculations

Template Usage:

{{ cycle.start_date }} - Cycle start date {{ cycle.end_date }} - Cycle end date {{ cycle.total_allowance }} - Total budget amount {{ total_spent }} - Amount spent so far {{ remaining_budget }} - Budget remaining {{ safe_daily_limit }} - Recommended daily spending limit {{ progress_percent }} - Progress bar percentage {{ today_spent }} - Today’s spending total {{ over_daily_limit }} - Warning flag for excess daily spending {{ status }} - Current cycle status

Conditional Display Examples:
{% if status == ‘no_cycle’ %}

<a href=”{% url ‘setCycle’ %}”>Set up your budget cycle</a>

{% endif %}

{% if over_daily_limit %}
<div class=”alert alert-warning”>

⚠️ You’ve exceeded your daily safe limit!

</div>

{% endif %}

{% if status == ‘overspent’ %}
<div class=”alert alert-danger”>

❌ You have exceeded your budget!

</div>

{% endif %}
